precepts.text: If a man put away his wife and she become another man's, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?
precepts.point: By the law, a woman who is put away and becomes another man's is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back defiles the land. The Most High does not permit it, but with no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: Her husband “went after her, to speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again”. But by the law: “If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man’s, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?” A woman who is put away and becomes another man’s is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back pollutes the land. The Most High does not permit it; but with no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did.

precepts.text: Her former husband may not take her again to be his wife after she is defiled, for that is abomination and causes the land to sin.
precepts.point: By the law, a woman who is put away and becomes another man's is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back defiles the land. The Most High does not permit it, but with no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: “Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before the Lord: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin”. The Levite going after his concubine to bring her again was the very thing the law forbids. Taking a woman back after she is defiled to her former husband is abomination and causes the land to sin; the Most High does not permit it. But there was no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, and this is what men did, with the damsel’s father rejoicing to meet him.

precepts.text: As for the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out, and the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.
precepts.point: Jerusalem is called Jebus here because the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, still dwelt in it; this is before David rose up and took it from them. When Israel came out of the wilderness, the promised land was inhabited primarily by Canaanites, and the children of Judah could not drive the Jebusites out.

precepts.why: Jerusalem is called Jebus here because the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, still dwelt in it: “As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.” When Israel came out of the wilderness the promised land was inhabited primarily by Canaanites, and Judah could not drive these out. So in the days of the judges the Levite passing by Jebus called it “the city of a stranger, that is not of the children of Israel”, and would not turn in there.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why:
This is before David rose up and took Jerusalem from the Jebusites. “And the king and his men went to Jerusalem unto the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land: which spake unto David, saying, Except thou take away the blind and the lame, thou shalt not come in hither: thinking, David cannot come in hither. Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David.” Not until king David went up against the Jebusites was the strong hold of Zion taken; that is when Jebus became the city of David.

In the Levite’s day it was still a city of strangers. That is why, even in those wild days, he would not lodge with heathens but passed over to lodge with his brothers in Gibeah or in Ramah.

precepts.text: The men of Sodom, old and young, all the people from every quarter, compassed Lot's house and said, bring them out unto us, that we may know them; the same words beaten at the door in Gibeah.
precepts.point: To know in this context is sexual intercourse; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old, the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and the scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why:
This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old. “the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter: And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.” The same words were beaten at the door in Gibeah: “Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.”

Certain sons of Belial, children of the devil, demon seed, beset the house round about in the middle of the night just as the men of Sodom compassed Lot’s house. All the tribes have some jacked up history somewhere down the line; this night is Benjamin’s.

precepts.text: Lot answered, do not so wickedly: behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; to know means no man had lain with them, so the knowing the men of Sodom sought was sexual.
precepts.point: To know in this context is sexual intercourse; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old, the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and the scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why:
Lot answered, “I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly. Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you”. To know means no man had lain with them, so the knowing the men of Sodom sought was sexual, and so was the knowing the men of Gibeah were howling for: the man himself.

The old man in Gibeah pleaded in the same words, “Nay, my brethren, nay, I pray you, do not so wickedly”, and like Lot he offered his maiden daughter and the concubine, “but unto this man do not so vile a thing.” The scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

precepts.text: They said, this one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge, and they pressed sore upon Lot and came near to break the door; sojourners in both cities were pressed the same way.
precepts.point: To know in this context is sexual intercourse; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old, the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and the scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: “And they said, Stand back. And they said again, This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge: now will we deal worse with thee, than with them. And they pressed sore upon the man, even Lot, and came near to break the door.” Sojourners in both cities were pressed the same way. Lot was a stranger dwelling in Sodom; the Levite was a traveller lodging one night in Gibeah, and the old man who took him in went out to a mob beating at his door. Gibeah of Benjamin did what Sodom did.

precepts.text: The vile thing named: God gave them up unto vile affections, the men leaving the natural use of the woman and burning in their lust one toward another, men with men working that which is unseemly. That is what Gibeah had on its mind.
precepts.point: To know in this context is sexual intercourse; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old, the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and the scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why:
The vile thing named. The men of Gibeah wanted the man, “that we may know him”, and the old man begged them, “unto this man do not so vile a thing.” Paul spells out what that vileness is: “God gave them up unto vile affections”, “the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly, and receiving in themselves that recompence of their error which was meet.”

That is what Gibeah had on its mind. These were sons of Belial, children of the devil, demon seed, doing in Israel what the men of Sodom did.

precepts.text: If a man force a betrothed damsel in the field and lie with her, the man only that lay with her shall die; forced means against her will, and the Most High made it punishable by death.
precepts.point: What we witnessed is rape, and the scripture is plain that rape is a sin worthy of death; marriage is the only honorable bed. Men out here calling themselves Israelites and teaching otherwise give Israelites a bad name; we preach the laws of the Most High.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: “they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning”. They is plural: this was a gang rape, forced, nothing voluntary about it, done in the anger of men who could not get the man they wanted. The law: “But if a man find a betrothed damsel in the field, and the man force her, and lie with her: then the man only that lay with her shall die”. Forced means against her will, and the Most High made it punishable by death. What we witnessed at Gibeah is rape, and the scripture is plain that rape is a sin worthy of death.

precepts.text: Unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing, for as when a man riseth against his neighbour and slayeth him, even so is this matter; the Most High counts rape the equivalent of murder, and in this gang rape the victim was literally murdered.

precepts.why: “But unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing; there is in the damsel no sin worthy of death: for as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him, even so is this matter”. The Most High counts rape the equivalent of murder, a man rising against his neighbour and slaying him. In this gang rape the victim was literally murdered: she fell down at the door with her hands upon the threshold, and when her lord said “Up, and let us be going”, none answered; there was no more spirit left in her. The sin is on the men of Gibeah, not on the woman.

points: Once more, there was no king in Israel, no leadership structure, still sheep without a shepherd. A certain Levite sojourning on the side of mount Ephraim took to him a concubine out of Bethlehemjudah; a concubine was a woman dealt with on the level of a servant.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: His concubine played the whore against him, laid with another man, then went away from him unto her father's house to Bethlehemjudah and was there four whole months.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: Instead of letting her go, her husband arose and went after her to speak friendly unto her and to bring her again, with his servant and a couple of asses, and the damsel's father rejoiced to meet him.

By the law, a woman who is put away and becomes another man's is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back defiles the land. The Most High does not permit it, but with no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The damsel's father retained him: eat, drink, lodge, three days, then a fourth, then a fifth. Like an old man who never has anybody to talk to, he kept finding a reason not to let the Levite go, and a one night plan stretched into five days.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The father's words on the fifth day cut a popular doctrine. They tarried until afternoon, and he said, behold, the day draweth toward evening, and then, behold, the day groweth to an end. According to the Bible the day ends at evening; and if it ends at evening it begins at evening, so a day runs from evening to evening, including the sabbath. That buries the sunrise to sunrise doctrine, which has no works and no fruits to show it was ever right.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The man would not tarry that night; five days was enough and he had business to tend to. He rose up, departed, and came over against Jebus, which is Jerusalem, with two saddled asses and his concubine.

Jerusalem is called Jebus here because the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, still dwelt in it; this is before David rose up and took it from them. When Israel came out of the wilderness, the promised land was inhabited primarily by Canaanites, and the children of Judah could not drive the Jebusites out.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: When the servant suggested turning in to lodge in this city of the Jebusites, his master refused: we will not turn aside hither into the city of a stranger, that is not of the children of Israel; we will pass over to Gibeah. Even in those wild days he would not lodge with heathens, only with his brothers.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The sun went down upon them by Gibeah, which belongeth to Benjamin, and when they went in and sat down in a street of the city, no man took them into his house to lodge. The Benjamites were not so friendly.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: An old man from his work out of the field at even, a man of mount Ephraim sojourning in Gibeah, lifted up his eyes and questioned the wayfaring man: whither goest thou? and whence comest thou? The Levite explained he was passing toward the house of the LORD with straw, provender, bread, and wine of his own, lacking nothing, yet no man would receive him to house.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The old man said, peace be with thee; howsoever let all thy wants lie upon me; only lodge not in the street. He knew the manner of the men of that city and what the streets of Gibeah held at night. He brought them into his house, and they washed their feet and did eat and drink.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: As they were making their hearts merry, certain sons of Belial, meaning children of the devil, demon seed, beset the house round about and beat at the door in the middle of the night, saying to the master of the house, bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.

To know in this context is sexual intercourse; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. This is a rerun of a very familiar story of old, the men of Sodom at Lot's door, and the scripture names exactly what vile thing they were after.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The master of the house went out and pleaded, nay, my brethren, do not so wickedly; seeing this man is come into mine house, do not this folly. Like Lot he offered his maiden daughter and the concubine, humble ye them, but unto this man do not so vile a thing. All the tribes have some jacked up history somewhere down the line; this night is Benjamin's.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: The men would not hearken, so the man brought his concubine forth unto them; and they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning. They is plural: this was a gang rape, forced, nothing voluntary about it, done in the anger of men who could not get the man they wanted.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: When the day began to spring they let her go, and the woman came in the dawning of the day and fell down at the door of the man's house where her lord was, her hands upon the threshold. In the morning he said, up, and let us be going; but none answered. There was no more spirit left in her; she was dead. He laid her upon an ass and got him unto his place.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: When he was come into his house he took a knife, laid hold on his concubine, and divided her, together with her bones, into twelve pieces, and sent her into all the coasts of Israel, to make the twelve tribes aware of what was done in Gibeah.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

points: All that saw it said, there was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds. The nation had never seen a matter like this, and it called the whole congregation to counsel.
